To determine if there are possible nonlinear relationships, we will consider fitting *decision trees* and *random forests*. These are mostly meant to be supplementary analysis and likely will not completely replace our multinomial logistic regression as the main model for association and inference.

As for generalised additive models, we may not want to use them for now since all our variables are categorical anyway so there really isn't anything to smooth.

```{r include = F}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, 
                      fig.align='center', fig.dim=c(10, 8))

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(randomForest)
library(caret)
library(mgcv)
library(knitr)
library(pdp)
```

# Classification Decision Tree

To start the tree analysis, we use a simple decision tree using `rpart`. We will mostly just use the full data set for now.

```{r}
# Load data set
fdat.full = readRDS(here("Objects", "fdat_full.rds")) %>% drop_na()

# Decision tree fit for ALT; need cp very small for something interesting...
res.alt = rpart(ALT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, data = fdat.full,
            control = rpart.control(cp = 0))
res.alt
printcp(res.alt)
res.alt.pruned = prune(res.alt, cp = 0.00081433)

# Plot
rpart.plot(res.alt.pruned, box.palette = "Greens", type = 2, fallen.leaves = T,
           tweak = 1.2, main = "ALT Decision Tree")
```

```{r}
# Decision tree fit for GGT
res.ggt = rpart(GGT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, data = fdat.full,
            control = rpart.control(cp = 0))
res.ggt
printcp(res.ggt) # tells us which gives smallest xerror
res.ggt.pruned = prune(res.ggt, cp = 0.00043029)

# Plot
rpart.plot(res.ggt.pruned, box.palette = "Greens", type = 2, fallen.leaves = T,
           tweak = 1.2, main = "GGT Decision Tree")
```

## Cross-Validation

```{r}
# ALT CV
set.seed(3888)
ctrl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 3, 
                    savePredictions = "final")
tree.cv.alt = train(ALT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB,
                    data = fdat.full, method = "rpart", trControl = ctrl,
                    tuneLength = 15, metric = "Accuracy")
tree.cv.alt
tree.cv.alt$bestTune
tree.cv.alt$results
plot(tree.cv.alt)
confusionMatrix(tree.cv.alt$pred$pred, tree.cv.alt$pred$obs)
```

```{r}
# ALT CV
set.seed(3888)
ctrl = trainControl(method = "repeatedcv", number = 10, repeats = 3,
                    savePredictions = "final")
tree.cv.ggt = train(GGT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB,
                    data = fdat.full, method = "rpart", trControl = ctrl,
                    tuneLength = 15, metric = "Accuracy")
tree.cv.ggt
tree.cv.ggt$bestTune
tree.cv.ggt$results
plot(tree.cv.ggt)
confusionMatrix(tree.cv.ggt$pred$pred, tree.cv.ggt$pred$obs)
```

However, trying to fit the final trees yields just one node, so I am not really sure if there is something wrong with the code or not. Essentially, it just classified everything as `Low`. So that could explain the respectable accuracy but terrible sensitivity for `Borderline`/`High`, at least for GGT. We also output the variable importance for the original pruned trees as well.

```{r}
# Final CV Trees
rpart.plot(tree.cv.alt$finalModel, box.palette = "Greens", 
           type = 2, fallen.leaves = TRUE, tweak = 1.2, 
           main = "ALT Final CV Decision Tree")
rpart.plot(tree.cv.ggt$finalModel, box.palette = "Greens", 
           type = 2, fallen.leaves = TRUE, tweak = 1.2, 
           main = "GGT Final CV Decision Tree")

# Original pruned trees variable importance
alt.vi = res.alt.pruned$variable.importance %>% as.data.frame()
colnames(alt.vi) = "Mean Decrease in Impurity"
ggt.vi = res.ggt.pruned$variable.importance %>% as.data.frame()
colnames(ggt.vi) = "Mean Decrease in Impurity"
kable(alt.vi, caption = "ALT Tree", digits = 3, align = "c")
kable(ggt.vi, caption = "GGT Tree", digits = 3, align = "c")
```

# Random Forests

We first start by fitting the random forest using the default `mtry`, which is 2 in our case.

```{r}
set.seed(3858)
# ALT
alt.rf = randomForest(ALT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, 
                      data = fdat.full,
                      importance = TRUE)
alt.rf
alt.class.error = 1 - confusionMatrix(fdat.full$ALT3, 
                                      predict(alt.rf, newdata = fdat.full, 
                                              type = "class"))$byClass[,"Recall"]
alt.class.error
alt.rf$importance
varImpPlot(alt.rf)

# GGT
ggt.rf = randomForest(GGT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, 
                      data = fdat.full,
                      importance = TRUE)
ggt.rf
ggt.class.error = 1 - confusionMatrix(fdat.full$GGT3, 
                                      predict(ggt.rf, newdata = fdat.full, 
                                              type = "class"))$byClass[,"Recall"]
ggt.class.error
ggt.rf$importance
varImpPlot(ggt.rf)
```

Next, we do cross-validation to determine the best `mtry`.

```{r}
set.seed(3888)

# ALT
ctrl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, savePredictions = "final")
if (file.exists(here("Objects", "alt_rf_train.rds"))) {
  
  alt.cv.rf = readRDS(here("Objects", "alt_rf_train.rds"))
  
} else {
  
  alt.cv.rf = train(ALT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, 
                  data = fdat.full, method = "rf", trControl = ctrl, 
                  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:5), ntree = 500,
                  importance = TRUE, metric = "Accuracy")
  saveRDS(alt.cv.rf, here("Objects", "alt_rf_train.rds"))
  
}
# CV tuning results
alt.cv.rf$results
alt.cv.rf$bestTune
plot(alt.cv.rf)
confusionMatrix(alt.cv.rf$pred$pred, alt.cv.rf$pred$obs)
varImp(alt.cv.rf)
```

```{r}
# GGT
set.seed(3888)
ctrl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10, savePredictions = "final")
if (file.exists(here("Objects", "ggt_rf_train.rds"))) {
  
  ggt.cv.rf = readRDS(here("Objects", "ggt_rf_train.rds"))
  
} else {
  
  ggt.cv.rf = train(GGT3 ~ EXREGUIC + AGEB + SEX + WAIST + DSMKHHRB, 
                  data = fdat.full, method = "rf", trControl = ctrl, 
                  tuneGrid = expand.grid(mtry = 1:5), ntree = 500,
                  importance = TRUE, metric = "Accuracy")
  saveRDS(ggt.cv.rf, here("Objects", "ggt_rf_train.rds"))
  
}
# CV tuning results
ggt.cv.rf$results
ggt.cv.rf$bestTune
plot(ggt.cv.rf)
confusionMatrix(ggt.cv.rf$pred$pred, ggt.cv.rf$pred$obs)
varImp(ggt.cv.rf)
```

The sensitivities overall say the same story as with decision trees, as it seems `Low` is heavily preferred in both cases especially for GGT.

## Partial Dependence Plots

We see the partial plots against `High` for each variable for now (a quick analysis showed that `Borderline` plots are roughly similar, but for brevity I will leave them off). We can expand to more higher-dimensional partial plots later on but for a quick analysis this should be enough to determine if there are nonlinear relationships at play here...

```{r}
# Using default RF mtry = 2; do for each variable
pdp.age.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = "AGEB", train = fdat.full,
                      which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.age.alt,
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on Age", xlab = "Age",
            ylab = "Partial Dependence")

pdp.sex.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = "SEX", train = fdat.full,
                      which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.sex.alt,
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on Sex", xlab = "Sex",
            ylab = "Partial Dependence")

pdp.waist.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = "WAIST", train = fdat.full,
                      which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.waist.alt,
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on Waist", xlab = "Waist",
            ylab = "Partial Dependence")

pdp.exercise.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = "EXREGUIC", train = fdat.full,
                      which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.exercise.alt,
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on EXREGUIC", xlab = "EXREGUIC",
            ylab = "Partial Dependence")

pdp.smoking.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = "DSMKHHRB", train = fdat.full,
                      which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.smoking.alt,
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on DSMKHHRB", xlab = "DSMKHHRB",
            ylab = "Partial Dependence")
```

Perhaps, we can do it with `EXREGUIC` and one of the variables, each time.

```{r}
# Contour plots
pdp.ex.waist.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = c("WAIST", "EXREGUIC"),
                           train = fdat.full, which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.ex.waist.alt, contour = TRUE, 
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on EXREGUIC and Waist")

pdp.ex.age.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = c("AGEB", "EXREGUIC"),
                           train = fdat.full, which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.ex.age.alt, contour = TRUE, 
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on EXREGUIC and Age")

pdp.ex.sex.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = c("SEX", "EXREGUIC"),
                           train = fdat.full, which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.ex.sex.alt, contour = TRUE, 
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on EXREGUIC and Sex")

pdp.ex.smoking.alt = partial(alt.rf, pred.var = c("DSMKHHRB", "EXREGUIC"),
                           train = fdat.full, which.class = "High", prob = TRUE)
plotPartial(pdp.ex.smoking.alt, contour = TRUE, 
            main = "Partial Dependence of High ALT on EXREGUIC and DSMKHHRB")
```
